es: Distinguir entre contar una emoción y mostrarla con acciones, reacciones del cuerpo y detalles de los sentidos, y repasar used to y would para hábitos del pasado.

teaching.en: Her hands began to tremble as she opened the letter, and she had to read the first line three times.
teaching.es: Las manos le empezaron a temblar al abrir la carta, y tuvo que leer la primera línea tres veces.
teaching.explanationEs: Muestra el nervio con una reacción del cuerpo, sin decir «she was nervous».
segments: Her hands began to tremble as she opened the letter,
and she had to read the first line three times.
teaching.audioText: Her hands began to tremble as she opened the letter, and she had to read the first line three times.

teaching.en: He slammed the door so hard that the glasses on the shelf rattled, and nobody dared to say a word.
teaching.es: Dio un portazo tan fuerte que los vasos de la estantería tintinearon, y nadie se atrevió a decir nada.
teaching.explanationEs: La acción y el sonido muestran la rabia sin nombrarla.
segments: He slammed the door so hard that the glasses on
the shelf rattled, and nobody dared to say a word.
teaching.audioText: He slammed the door so hard that the glasses on the shelf rattled, and nobody dared to say a word.

teaching.en: Across the table, Leo would fidget with his spoon and avoid eye contact whenever the subject of money came up.
teaching.es: Al otro lado de la mesa, Leo jugueteaba con la cuchara y evitaba mirar a los ojos cada vez que salía el tema del dinero.
teaching.explanationEs: Would + verbo base describe una conducta repetida en el pasado; los gestos muestran la incomodidad.
segments: Across the table, Leo would fidget with his spoon and
avoid eye contact whenever the subject of money came up.
teaching.audioText: Across the table, Leo would fidget with his spoon and avoid eye contact whenever the subject of money came up.

teaching.en: When he was angry, my grandfather would clench his fists and count the seconds under his breath before answering.
teaching.es: Cuando se enojaba, mi abuelo apretaba los puños y contaba los segundos en voz baja antes de contestar.
teaching.explanationEs: Dos acciones concretas muestran el autocontrol; contar sería «he tried to stay calm».
segments: When he was angry, my grandfather would clench his fists
and count the seconds under his breath before answering.
teaching.audioText: When he was angry, my grandfather would clench his fists and count the seconds under his breath before answering.

teaching.en: When burnt toast fills a silent kitchen, add a lump in your throat and readers feel the tension without being told.
teaching.es: Cuando la tostada quemada llena una cocina en silencio, añade un nudo en la garganta y los lectores sentirán la tensión sin que se la cuenten.
teaching.explanationEs: Un detalle del olfato, el silencio y una sensación del cuerpo muestran la tensión.
segments: When burnt toast fills a silent kitchen, add a lump in
your throat and readers feel the tension without being told.
teaching.audioText: When burnt toast fills a silent kitchen, add a lump in your throat and readers feel the tension without being told.

teaching.en: If you fidget, bite your nails and keep checking the clock, readers feel your anxiety without ever being told about it.
teaching.es: Si te mueves sin parar, te muerdes las uñas y miras el reloj todo el tiempo, los lectores sienten tu ansiedad sin que nadie se la cuente.
teaching.explanationEs: Varias acciones pequeñas y concretas muestran una emoción mejor que una palabra abstracta.
segments: If you fidget, bite your nails and keep checking the clock,
readers feel your anxiety without ever being told about it.
teaching.audioText: If you fidget, bite your nails and keep checking the clock, readers feel your anxiety without ever being told about it.

prompt.es: ¿Qué frase muestra la rabia de Tom en lugar de contarla?

choices.text: Tom slammed the door so hard that the glasses rattled.
Tom was so angry that he could not speak.
Tom's anger was obvious to everybody in the room.

feedback.es: El portazo y el tintineo de los vasos son una acción y un sonido que el lector percibe; las otras frases siguen nombrando la emoción.

hint.es: Busca la acción concreta con sonido, no la etiqueta «angry».

origin.text: In a writing workshop, the teacher asks the students to replace the line “Tom was angry” with something the reader can see or hear, without naming the emotion.

prompt.es: Completa: «Su voz empezó a temblar de enojo al leer el mensaje en voz alta.»

feedback.es: La causa de una reacción del cuerpo se introduce normalmente con with: tremble with anger. «Of» sería un calco del español; in anger también se oye, pero with es la forma habitual.

hint.es: La preposición que introduce la causa de una reacción.

origin.text: Sara did not shout. Her voice began to tremble ___ anger as she read the message aloud, and nobody in the room moved.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Solía contar los segundos hasta que pasaba el tren nocturno.»

answer.text: He would count the seconds until the night train passed
accepted: He would count the seconds until the night train passed
Until the night train passed, he would count the seconds

feedback.es: Would + verbo base describe una conducta repetida en el pasado; count the seconds se mantiene junto como colocación.

hint.es: Would va seguido del verbo base, sin to.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada frase con lo que hace el narrador.

He slammed the door so hard that the windows rattled.

pairs.es: Muestra rabia con acción y sonido

pairs: The smell of burnt toast filled the silent kitchen.

pairs.es: Muestra tensión con olor y silencio

pairs: She was very nervous about the exam.

feedback.es: Las tres primeras ofrecen detalles que el lector percibe; la última nombra la emoción y por eso cuenta.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué emoción muestra la escena sin nombrarla.

choices.text: Quiet sadness after a painful argument.
Bored waiting while dinner is being prepared.
Hidden anger that one of them cannot express.
Anxious waiting for news that may change everything.

feedback.es: El silencio, el reloj, el teléfono que nadie coge y la mano que tiembla muestran ansiedad ante una noticia esperada; ninguna frase nombra la emoción.

origin.audio: The kitchen smelled of burnt toast. Nobody spoke. Leo sat with his coat still on, tapping the table, and Ana kept her eyes on the clock. When the phone finally rang, neither of them moved. Leo took a long breath, and his hand, just for a moment, began to tremble.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Se mordía las uñas y evitaba mirar a los ojos.»

answer.text: She bit her nails and avoided eye contact

feedback.es: Dos acciones concretas muestran incomodidad; avoid eye contact se mantiene junto como colocación.

prompt.es: Reescribe las tres frases mostrando la emoción con una acción o un gesto.

answer.text: Leo stared at the floor and avoided eye contact as everybody laughed. Mia bit her nails, tapped her foot and read the same line of the letter three times. Ana slammed the door so hard that the glasses rattled.
accepted: Leo stared at the floor and avoided eye contact as everybody laughed. Mia bit her nails, tapped her foot and read the same line of the letter three times. Ana slammed the door so hard that the glasses rattled.
Leo looked away and said nothing while the others laughed. Mia began to fidget, and her hands started to tremble as she checked the clock. Ana clenched her fists and slammed the door behind her.
Leo kept his eyes on the floor while the room laughed. Mia kept checking the clock, and she began to bite her nails. Ana slammed her hand on the table and left the room.

feedback.es: Mostrar es dar un gesto o una reacción concreta: Leo mirando al suelo; Mia mordiéndose las uñas o mirando el reloj; Ana con un portazo o los puños apretados.

origin.text: Frases que cuentan: «Leo was embarrassed. Mia was nervous. Ana was angry.» Reescríbelas mostrando cada emoción con una acción, un gesto o una reacción del cuerpo (sin usar embarrassed, nervous ni angry).

evidenceGroups: kept his eyes on the floor

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué sugiere el detalle de los puños apretados.

choices.text: That he had been tense all day without noticing it.
That he was angry with his daughter for coming home late.
That he was trying to hide his anger from her.
That he was still cross with her for not calling.

feedback.es: El aliento retenido y «only then did he notice» indican una tensión acumulada de la que no era consciente; la sonrisa de ella lo libera. El texto no habla de enojo.

origin.audio: The house was silent except for the clock in the hall. Carlos waited by the window with his jacket still on, although he had been home for an hour. On the table, his coffee had gone cold. Every few minutes he picked up the phone, looked at it and put it down again. When his daughter finally came in, he started to speak, and stopped. She smiled. He let out a breath that seemed to have been waiting all day, and only then did he notice that his fists were clenched.

prompt.es: Completa: «Nadie podía ignorar el olor a tostada quemada que venía de la cocina.»

feedback.es: Burnt toast es el detalle sensorial clásico para una tensión que nadie menciona; burned es la variante americana y burning toast también es natural.

origin.text: It was a small flat, and nobody could ignore the smell of ___ toast that drifted in from the kitchen while the argument went on.

prompt.es: ¿Qué sugiere el comentario de la profesora sobre el primer borrador?

choices.text: That a character should never feel more than one emotion.
That naming emotions is weaker than showing what causes them.
That the draft needs fewer details about the interview.
That Sara's father should appear in the scene.

feedback.es: La profesora no discute las emociones, sino que el lector no las siente: nombrarlas no basta, hay que mostrar lo que las provoca y lo que hacen.

origin.text: Mia's first draft read: “Sara was very nervous. She was worried about the interview. She was sad because her father could not come. She was also angry with herself.” Her teacher wrote on the page: “Four emotions, and I don't feel any of them.”

prompt.es: ¿Qué sugiere el último detalle del narrador sobre la casa?

choices.text: That the father has become very strict about cleaning.
That the children no longer want to visit the house.
That something painful has changed in the family.
That the house has simply been cleaned from top to bottom.

feedback.es: El contraste entre el pasado (olor, tarareo) y el presente (nada, ventanas cerradas, nadie tararea) sugiere una pérdida sin nombrarla.

origin.text: When we were children, the house used to be full of the scent of pine and wet wool, and my mother would hum while she counted the seconds on the kitchen clock. Now it smells of nothing at all. My father keeps the windows shut, even in July, and nobody hums.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige por qué acepta ahora la profesora el texto de Leo.

choices.text: Because the new version is longer than the first draft.
Because Mia's action is more polite than her first reaction.
Because Leo has chosen a stronger word than angry.
Because the reader now sees the anger instead of being told.

feedback.es: La profesora lo dice con sus palabras: ve la rabia y Leo ni siquiera usó la palabra. Mostrar convence más que nombrar.

origin.audio: Leo showed his teacher his first draft: Mia was angry. The teacher sighed. “Show me,” she said. So Leo wrote it again: Mia got up so fast that her chair fell over, picked up her bag and left without a word. The teacher read it twice. “Now I believe you,” she said. “I can see the anger, and you never even used the word.”

prompt.es: Completa: «Contábamos los segundos hasta que sonaba el timbre.»

feedback.es: Count the seconds es la colocación que se usa para esperar con impaciencia; used to + verbo base marca el hábito del pasado.

origin.text: At the end of the lesson we used to ___ the seconds until the bell rang, and our teacher would pretend not to notice.

es: Controlar el ritmo narrativo con anteposición de lugar (Down the hill ran the dog), adverbios negativos con inversión (Never had she seen…), fragmentos intencionados y frases de longitud variada.

teaching.en: Down the hill ran the dog, and behind it, carried on the wind, came the distant barking of another.
teaching.es: Colina abajo corrió el perro, y detrás de él, llevados por el viento, llegaron los ladridos lejanos de otro.
teaching.explanationEs: Anteposición: lugar + verbo + sujeto. El sujeto es un nombre (the dog), así que el verbo va antes.
segments: Down the hill ran the dog, and behind it, carried
on the wind, came the distant barking of another.
teaching.audioText: Down the hill ran the dog, and behind it, carried on the wind, came the distant barking of another.

teaching.en: On the table lay a single letter, and beside it, in the half-dark, lay the key nobody had touched for years.
teaching.es: Sobre la mesa yacía una sola carta, y junto a ella, en la penumbra, estaba la llave que nadie había tocado en años.
teaching.explanationEs: Con verbos de posición como lay, stood o hung la inversión es natural: lugar + verbo + sujeto.
segments: On the table lay a single letter, and beside it, in
the half-dark, lay the key nobody had touched for years.
teaching.audioText: On the table lay a single letter, and beside it, in the half-dark, lay the key nobody had touched for years.

teaching.en: Up the stairs came muffled footsteps, and every step made the old boards creak as though the house were complaining.
teaching.es: Escaleras arriba llegaron unos pasos apagados, y cada paso hacía crujir las viejas tablas como si la casa se quejara.
teaching.explanationEs: Los sonidos se prestan a la anteposición: el lector oye primero el lugar y después el sujeto.
segments: Up the stairs came muffled footsteps, and every step made
the old boards creak as though the house were complaining.
teaching.audioText: Up the stairs came muffled footsteps, and every step made the old boards creak as though the house were complaining.

teaching.en: Motionless she stood at the gate, and in the whole lane there was not a soul to hear her call.
teaching.es: Inmóvil se quedó junto a la verja, y en todo el camino no había ni un alma que oyera su llamada.
teaching.explanationEs: Si el sujeto es un pronombre no hay inversión: Motionless she stood. El adjetivo al inicio pone el énfasis en el estado.
segments: Motionless she stood at the gate, and in the whole
lane there was not a soul to hear her call.
teaching.audioText: Motionless she stood at the gate, and in the whole lane there was not a soul to hear her call.

teaching.en: Never had he known a deathly silence like that one; out of nowhere, the whole hill seemed to fall silent.
teaching.es: Nunca había conocido un silencio sepulcral como ese; de repente, toda la colina parecía quedarse callada.
teaching.explanationEs: Never al inicio pide inversión: never + auxiliar + sujeto (had he).
segments: Never had he known a deathly silence like that one;
out of nowhere, the whole hill seemed to fall silent.
teaching.audioText: Never had he known a deathly silence like that one; out of nowhere, the whole hill seemed to fall silent.

teaching.en: She walked for hours through the empty streets, chilled to the bones, and found only an eerie calm. Then she stopped.
teaching.es: Caminó durante horas por las calles vacías, helada hasta los huesos, y solo encontró una calma inquietante. Entonces se detuvo.
teaching.explanationEs: Una frase larga que fluye y una corta que golpea crean ritmo; la corta funciona como un fragmento.
segments: She walked for hours through the empty streets, chilled to the
bones, and found only an eerie calm. Then she stopped.
teaching.audioText: She walked for hours through the empty streets, chilled to the bones, and found only an eerie calm. Then she stopped.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Por el sendero subieron unos pasos apagados.»

answer.text: Up the path came muffled footsteps

feedback.es: Lugar + verbo + sujeto: el sujeto es un nombre (muffled footsteps), así que came va antes de él.

hint.es: Empieza por el lugar; el verbo precede al sujeto.

prompt.es: ¿Qué versión antepone correctamente el lugar cuando el sujeto es «it»?

choices.text: Down the lane ran it, barking at nothing.
Down it the lane ran, barking at nothing.
Down the lane did it run, barking at nothing.
Down the lane it ran, barking at nothing.

feedback.es: Con un pronombre como sujeto no hay inversión: lugar + pronombre + verbo. Las demás versiones alteran el orden sin motivo.

hint.es: Con pronombre, el sujeto va antes del verbo.

origin.text: Mia is revising a scene in which her dog gets out of the gate and runs down the lane. Because the subject will be the pronoun it, she has to choose the right word order.

prompt.es: Completa: «Nunca había visto una calle tan silenciosa.»

feedback.es: Never al inicio exige auxiliar + sujeto: never had she seen. Sin la inversión la frase sería un calco del español.

hint.es: Tras never, el auxiliar del past perfect va antes del sujeto.

origin.text: The cold reached her bones as she crossed the square. Never ___ she seen such a silent street, and not a soul was around.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada frase con el recurso de ritmo que usa.

pairs: Down the hill ran the dog.
Down the hill it ran.
Never had she seen such a view.
Silence. Then footsteps.

feedback.es: Cada frase altera el orden de una manera distinta: inversión con nombre, pronombre sin inversión, adverbio negativo y fragmentos.

pairs: Down the hill ran the dog.
Down the hill it ran.
Never had she seen such a view.
Silence. Then footsteps.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué efecto crean las frases cortas del final.

choices.text: They slow the pace and build tension after the long sentence.
They add more information about the streets she crossed.
They suggest that the narrator is tired of describing.
They explain why she had walked for hours.

feedback.es: La frase larga fluye como el paseo; las cortas (Silence. A dog… footsteps.) frenan el ritmo y crean tensión. No añaden datos ni explican nada.

origin.audio: She walked for hours through the empty streets, past closed shops and dark windows, until the cold reached her bones. Then she stopped. Silence. A dog, somewhere far off. And then, slowly, footsteps. She did not look back.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Inmóvil, se quedó junto a la verja, sin un alma alrededor.»

answer.text: Motionless she stood at the gate, not a soul around
accepted: Motionless she stood at the gate, not a soul around
She stood motionless at the gate, not a soul around

feedback.es: Con pronombre no hay inversión (Motionless she stood); el adjetivo al inicio da énfasis, aunque también es posible colocarlo tras el verbo.

prompt.es: Reescribe el párrafo con anteposición de lugar, never + inversión y dos fragmentos.

answer.text: At the gate stood a young woman. Up the hill ran the old dog. Never had she heard such a silent night. Silence. Then a creak.
accepted: At the gate stood a young woman. Up the hill ran the old dog. Never had she heard such a silent night. Silence. Then a creak.
By the gate stood a young woman. Up the hill raced the old dog. Never before had she heard such a silent night. Silence. A creak.

feedback.es: El párrafo mejora con lugar + verbo + sujeto (At the gate stood…), never + inversión (Never had she heard…) y dos fragmentos que golpean (Silence. Then a creak.).

origin.text: Párrafo: «A young woman stood at the gate. The old dog ran up the hill. She had never heard such a silent night. There was silence. Then there was a creak.» Reescríbelo con una anteposición de lugar con inversión, una frase con Never had y dos fragmentos sin verbo.

evidenceGroups: silence then the sound of a creak

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué sugiere el cambio de ritmo al final del pasaje.

choices.text: That the group has finally reached the safety of camp.
That the group senses a danger it cannot yet see.
That the group is arguing about which way to go.
That the danger is over now that the wind has dropped.

feedback.es: Las frases largas reflejan la marcha monótona; al final, los fragmentos (A deathly silence. Another. Down.), el viento que cae y las piedras que se desprenden anuncian un peligro que el grupo aún no ve. Nadie discute y nada indica que el peligro haya pasado.

origin.audio: The group had been climbing since dawn, and by midday the top of the hill had disappeared into cloud. Up the path they walked, step after tired step, each of them chilled to the bones, each of them counting the hours until camp. Below them, the valley had vanished completely, and the path behind them was already gone. Nobody spoke. Then, out of nowhere, the wind dropped. A deathly silence. Somewhere above them, a rock fell. Another. Motionless, they listened. Carlos was the first to move. He raised one hand and whispered a single word. Down.

prompt.es: Completa: «Apenas había cerrado la puerta cuando se apagaron las luces.»

feedback.es: Hardly al inicio exige la misma inversión que never: hardly had she closed… when. El past perfect marca lo anterior.

origin.text: It was past midnight, and the flat was quiet. Hardly ___ she closed the door when every light in the building went out.

prompt.es: ¿Con qué propósito termina el autor con una frase muy corta?

choices.text: To confirm that she had prepared everything well.
To hint that her sister had talked her out of it.
To surprise the reader with an unexpected twist.
To summarise the long preparation in a short phrase.

feedback.es: La frase larga acumula preparativos y la corta los contradice: el contraste de ritmo produce un giro inesperado. El texto no menciona a la hermana.

origin.text: She had spent three years planning the route, saving every spare cent, studying the maps until she could have drawn them from memory, and telling nobody, not even her sister, what she intended to do with the money. On the morning of the departure, the suitcase was already packed. She did not go.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Nunca antes había oído un silencio tan profundo.»

answer.text: Never before had I heard such a deep silence

feedback.es: Never before al inicio pide inversión: auxiliar + sujeto (had I). El énfasis recae en lo excepcional de la experiencia.

prompt.es: ¿Qué efecto logran las anteposiciones de este fragmento?

choices.text: They speed the scene up by cutting extra words.
They show that the guests know the stranger well.
They reveal that the narrator is one of the guests.
They delay the subject and focus attention on the stranger.

feedback.es: La inversión (At the door stood…, Never had the room…) retrasa el sujeto y lo destaca: el lector se centra en el desconocido y en el silencio.

origin.text: The party was going well when the music stopped. At the door stood a man nobody had invited. Never had the room been so quiet. Slowly, he took off his hat. Then, in a voice that seemed to come from another age, he asked for a glass of water.

prompt.es: Completa: «Toda la calle se quedó callada al pasar el desconocido.»

feedback.es: Fall silent es la colocación para quedarse callado de pronto; fall quiet también es posible, pero es más coloquial.

origin.text: The whole street seemed to fall ___ as the stranger walked past, and nobody dared to ask him who he was.

es: Reconstruir el orden real de los hechos en una anécdota que salta entre tiempos, distinguiendo la línea principal del fondo anterior y de lo que sucedería después.

teaching.en: Years earlier, her father had promised to take her to the city, and she had never forgotten it.
teaching.es: Años antes, su padre le había prometido llevarla a la ciudad, y ella nunca lo había olvidado.
teaching.explanationEs: Past perfect (had promised): un hecho anterior al momento que se cuenta; years earlier lo señala.
segments: Years earlier, her father had promised to take her
to the city, and she had never forgotten it.
teaching.audioText: Years earlier, her father had promised to take her to the city, and she had never forgotten it.

teaching.en: By the time the last train arrived, my grandmother had been waiting on the station platform for her cousin for nearly two hours.
teaching.es: Para cuando llegó el último tren, mi abuela llevaba casi dos horas esperando a su prima en el andén de la estación.
teaching.explanationEs: Past perfect continuous (had been waiting): una actividad en curso antes del hecho principal (arrived).
segments: By the time the last train arrived, my grandmother had been waiting
on the station platform for her cousin for nearly two hours.
teaching.audioText: By the time the last train arrived, my grandmother had been waiting on the station platform for her cousin for nearly two hours.

teaching.en: A stranger offered her his umbrella, and they talked until the rain stopped and the lamps came on along the street.
teaching.es: Un desconocido le ofreció su paraguas, y hablaron hasta que dejó de llover y se encendieron las farolas de la calle.
teaching.explanationEs: Los hechos principales van en past simple y en orden: offered, talked, stopped, came on.
segments: A stranger offered her his umbrella, and they talked until the
rain stopped and the lamps came on along the street.
teaching.audioText: A stranger offered her his umbrella, and they talked until the rain stopped and the lamps came on along the street.

teaching.en: She did not know it then, but she would marry him three years later, and they would tie the knot in the village church.
teaching.es: Entonces no lo sabía, pero se casaría con él tres años después, y darían el sí en la iglesia del pueblo.
teaching.explanationEs: Would + verbo anticipa lo posterior al momento del relato, visto desde el pasado.
segments: She did not know it then, but she would marry him three
years later, and they would tie the knot in the village church.
teaching.audioText: She did not know it then, but she would marry him three years later, and they would tie the knot in the village church.

teaching.en: As it turned out, the stranger was her cousin's friend, a fact that would only come to light at the wedding.
teaching.es: Como resultó ser, el desconocido era amigo de su prima, algo que solo saldría a la luz en la boda.
teaching.explanationEs: As it turned out presenta un hecho sorprendente que cambia lo que el oyente creía saber.
segments: As it turned out, the stranger was her cousin's friend, a
fact that would only come to light at the wedding.
teaching.audioText: As it turned out, the stranger was her cousin's friend, a fact that would only come to light at the wedding.

teaching.en: When the old man was about to pass away, he asked the family to keep the umbrella that had started the whole story.
teaching.es: Cuando el anciano estaba a punto de fallecer, pidió a la familia que conservara el paraguas que había comenzado toda la historia.
teaching.explanationEs: Was about to + verbo base: estaba a punto de; had started sitúa el paraguas antes de ese momento.
segments: When the old man was about to pass away, he asked the
family to keep the umbrella that had started the whole story.
teaching.audioText: When the old man was about to pass away, he asked the family to keep the umbrella that had started the whole story.

prompt.es: Según este fragmento, ¿qué ocurrió primero en la cronología real?

choices.text: Her father promised to take her to the city.
She waited for two hours on the platform.
A stranger offered her his umbrella.
The last train arrived at the station.

feedback.es: Years earlier y el past perfect (had promised) sitúan la promesa antes de todo lo demás; la espera, el tren y el paraguas son posteriores.

hint.es: Busca el marcador que lleva más atrás en el tiempo.

origin.text: By the time the last train arrived, my grandmother had been waiting on the station platform for two hours. Years earlier, her father had promised to take her to the city. A stranger offered her his umbrella, and they talked until the rain stopped.

prompt.es: Completa: «Cuando llegó el autobús, Sara llevaba dos horas esperando.»

As it turned out, I never returned it: she passed away before I came home. That watch would stay in my pocket for sixty years. Now it is yours.” I had never seen him so serious. The room went quiet, and even the children stopped playing.

prompt.es: Escribe una anécdota de unas 150 palabras con escena, giro y desenlace.

answer.text: It was a grey afternoon, and the rain was tapping on the windows of the library. I was about to return a book when I noticed a small note between the pages. Suddenly, my curiosity woke up. It was a phone number, and below it someone had written: “Call me if you find this.” I was going to throw the note away, but then I remembered how quiet the library could feel on a wet day, so I phoned. A woman answered at once. “Finally,” she said, laughing. “I left it there three years ago, as a joke.” We talked for an hour. Little did I know that she would become my business partner, and that we would open a small shop together. To my relief, the shop was an immediate success, and the note is still on the wall.
accepted: It was a grey afternoon, and the rain was tapping on the windows of the library. I was about to return a book when I noticed a small note between the pages. Suddenly, my curiosity woke up. It was a phone number, and below it someone had written: “Call me if you find this.” I was going to throw the note away, but then I remembered how quiet the library could feel on a wet day, so I phoned. A woman answered at once. “Finally,” she said, laughing. “I left it there three years ago, as a joke.” We talked for an hour. Little did I know that she would become my business partner, and that we would open a small shop together. To my relief, the shop was an immediate success, and the note is still on the wall.

It was a rainy evening, and the wind was blowing hard outside the station. A few people were waiting quietly in the dark. I was about to get on the last bus when it dawned on me that my wallet was not in my bag. My heart was beating very fast. I was going to ask the driver for help, but a young woman handed me a ticket. “Don't worry,” she said. “Buy me a coffee one day.” I thanked her and sat by the window. Little did I know that I would meet her again. Two weeks later, she came into my new office, and she would become my best friend for the rest of my life, and my business partner too.

feedback.es: Una buena anécdota abre con una escena en pasado continuo, la rompe con un hecho, usa was about to / was going to y anticipa el final con would (Little did I know…).

Giro: la persona que contestó resultó ser tu futura socia. Little did I know that Mr Hall owned the company where I had applied for a job. As luck would have it, he remembered my face on the day of the interview, and within a month I had signed my contract.

prompt.es: Cuenta la anécdota (unas 170 palabras) y responde a las dos preguntas del público.

answer.text:
Every summer, the whole family used to meet at my grandmother's house. The kitchen smelled of coffee, and the relatives were all talking at once. My aunt Mia would always tell the same story about the day she lost her umbrella at the station. That year, she was about to start it again when a stranger walked into the garden, holding an old umbrella. Nobody recognised him. Silence. Then my aunt stood up and put her hand to her face. “It's mine,” she whispered. He had been looking for her for thirty years, and he had kept the umbrella in his house all that time. Little did we know that he would stay for dinner, and that he would become part of the family.
Did you recognise him? No, I didn't. I thought he was a neighbour.
What did your aunt say? Fair enough, she said. Tonight, for once, we will hear a new story.

When I was a child, we would all meet at my grandmother's house on Sundays. The kitchen smelled of bread, and the relatives were laughing in the garden. My aunt Mia used to tell the same story about the day she lost her umbrella at the station. One Sunday, she was about to begin when a tall man walked into the garden with an umbrella in his hand. Nobody knew him. Silence. Then my aunt smiled and opened her arms. “That's my umbrella,” she said. He had been searching for her for thirty years, and he had never given up. Little did I know that he would become my uncle's best friend.
Did you recognise him? No, I didn't. I thought he was a friend of my uncle.
What did your aunt say? Honestly, she said nothing. She just hugged him.

origin.text: Situación: reunión familiar en casa de tu abuela. Cada verano tu tía Mia contaba la historia del día que perdió su paraguas en la estación. Un año, iba a empezar cuando un desconocido entró en el jardín con un paraguas viejo: era el hombre que lo había encontrado hacía treinta años y llevaba todo ese tiempo buscándola. Cuenta la anécdota (unas 170 palabras) con: un hábito o escena del pasado (used to / would), un hecho con was about to, un giro con had been o Little did we know y un final corto. Después responde a dos preguntas del público: «Did you recognise him?» y «What did your aunt say?».

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué sugiere el final sobre la actitud de la familia.

choices.text: That the family cares more about the tradition than about the story itself.
That the family had finally grown tired of the story.
That the uncle was losing his memory and they were worried.
That the cousins secretly preferred a different story.

feedback.es: Nadie lo ayudó porque querían oírlo encontrar el final: lo que valoran es la costumbre de escucharlo, no los detalles de la historia.

origin.audio: Every year, at the family reunion, my uncle Carlos would tell the same story about the night he met my aunt. He would embellish it a little more each time, until the rain became a storm and the walk became a mountain climb. The distant relatives would smile politely, and my cousins would count the new details. Yet nobody ever stopped him. When he reached the punchline, the whole table burst out laughing, even those who could have told it word for word. Last year he forgot the ending. Nobody helped him. For once, we all just wanted to hear him find it.

prompt.es: Completa: «Adorna sus historias: cada vez que las cuenta, el pez crece.»

feedback.es: Embellish es la palabra precisa para adornar un relato; exaggerate y embroider también son posibles, pero embellish subraya el adorno más que la exageración.

origin.text: Every time he tells it, the fish gets bigger. He likes to ___ his stories a little, and nobody minds.

prompt.es: ¿Qué da a entender la pausa de Ana en esta conversación?

choices.text: That she has forgotten what happened that night.
That she is exaggerating to keep the audience laughing.
That she is embarrassed about what she ate.
That she does not want to answer his question.

feedback.es: La pausa y «Let's say I got carried away» revelan que adorna la respuesta para divertir; la risa posterior confirma que el público entiende el juego.

origin.text: “Did you really eat it?” asked Leo. “Every bit,” said Ana. “Even the candles?” “Well...” She looked at the ceiling. “Let's say I got carried away.” For a second nobody laughed. Then the whole table burst out laughing, and Leo laughed too.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Toda la mesa se echó a reír al oír el remate.»

answer.text: The whole table burst out laughing at the punchline

feedback.es: Burst out laughing se mantiene junto; at the punchline indica el momento exacto de la reacción.

prompt.es: ¿Cuál es la postura del autor sobre las historias familiares?

choices.text: That they should be checked against the real facts.
That they reveal more about the family than the event, which is a problem.
That they need not be strictly accurate to be worth telling.
That a good punchline matters more than any other detail.

feedback.es: «Yet that, surely, is the point» defiende que la inexactitud es lo que da sentido a estas historias: no buscan informar, sino reflejar a la familia, y el autor no lo lamenta.

origin.text: Family stories are rarely accurate. Every retelling embellishes them, drops the awkward details and improves the punchline, until the tale says more about the family than about the event. Yet that, surely, is the point: nobody at a reunion wants a report; they want to hear themselves described, a little taller and a little funnier than they were.

prompt.es: Completa: «La broma podría haber salido mal, pero mi tía supo verle el lado gracioso.»

feedback.es: Backfire describe algo que sale al revés de lo previsto; failed no expresa ese efecto contrario y suena menos natural.
